items.title: BODMAS, Simplification & Defined Symbols
items.body:
**BODMAS** fixes the order of operations in any expression:

| Order | Operation |
|---|---|
| B | Brackets — ( ), { }, [ ] inner-first |
| O | Orders — powers & roots |
| D M | Division & Multiplication — **left to right** (equal rank) |
| A S | Addition & Subtraction — **left to right** |

**Worked example:** 48 ÷ 8 × 3 + (7 − 4)² − 5
= 48 ÷ 8 × 3 + 3² − 5 → 6 × 3 + 9 − 5 → 18 + 9 − 5 = **22**.

**Defined-symbol (operator) questions:** replace the invented symbol with its rule, then apply BODMAS. E.g. if a △ b = (a + b) ÷ (a − b), then 9 △ 5 = 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5. Respect operand order — a △ b ≠ b △ a in general.

**Common trap:** doing × before ÷ (or + before −). They are equal in rank and evaluated left to right.
keyPoints: BODMAS = Brackets, Orders, Division/Multiplication (left→right), Addition/Subtraction (left→right).
Division and multiplication share one rank; solve whichever comes first from the left.
In defined-symbol problems, substitute the rule exactly before simplifying.
a △ b need not equal b △ a — operand order matters.
Always resolve innermost brackets and powers before ÷/× and +/−.

items.title: Algebraic Identities — the standard toolkit
items.body:
Memorise these; most 'find a² + b²' or 'find a³ + b³' problems use them directly.

| Identity | Form |
|---|---|
| Square of sum | (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² |
| Square of difference | (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² |
| Difference of squares | a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) |
| Sum of cubes | a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) |
| Difference of cubes | a³ − b³ = (a − b)³ + 3ab(a − b) |
| Three-term square | (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca) |

**Worked example:** a + b = 7, ab = 10 ⇒ a³ + b³ = 7³ − 3(10)(7) = 343 − 210 = **133**.

**Shortcut:** a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab, and a² + b² = (a − b)² + 2ab — pick whichever data you are given.

**Common trap:** forgetting the factor of 2 on the ab term (writing (a+b)² = a² + ab + b²).
keyPoints: (a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b² — never drop the 2ab term.
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab = (a − b)² + 2ab.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b); a³ − b³ = (a − b)³ + 3ab(a − b).
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca).

items.title: Linear & Quadratic Equations
items.body:
**Linear (one variable):** expand brackets, transpose terms (sign flips across '='), divide by the coefficient last. e.g. 3(x + 4) = 5x − 2 ⇒ 3x + 12 = 5x − 2 ⇒ 14 = 2x ⇒ x = 7.

**Linear (two variables):** solve by substitution or elimination, then verify in BOTH equations. e.g. 4x + 3y = 25, 2x − y = 5 ⇒ y = 2x − 5 ⇒ 10x − 15 = 25 ⇒ x = 4, y = 3.

**Quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0:**
- Roots by factorisation (split middle term) or formula x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a.
- **Discriminant D = b² − 4ac** decides nature:

| D | Nature of roots |
|---|---|
| D > 0 | Real & distinct |
| D = 0 | Real & equal |
| D < 0 | Imaginary (complex) |

- **Sum of roots = −b/a, Product = c/a.**

**Worked example:** x² − 6x + 11 = 0 ⇒ D = 36 − 44 = −8 < 0 ⇒ roots imaginary; sum = 6, product = 11.

**Common trap:** forgetting the sign of b in −b/a, or mislabelling factor numbers as roots (roots take the opposite sign of the split numbers).
keyPoints: Transpose across '=' by flipping the sign; divide by the x-coefficient last.
Verify a two-variable solution in BOTH original equations.
Quadratic roots: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a.
Discriminant D = b² − 4ac: >0 real distinct, =0 real equal, <0 imaginary.
Sum of roots = −b/a; product of roots = c/a.

items.title: Progressions — AP, GP, HP & AGP
items.body:
| Type | nth term | Sum |
|---|---|---|
| AP | aₙ = a + (n − 1)d | Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (a + l) |
| GP | aₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹ | Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); S∞ = a/(1 − r) if \|r\| < 1 |
| HP | reciprocals form an AP | convert to AP, solve, invert |

**GP worked example:** 3, 6, 12, … first 8 terms: a = 3, r = 2 ⇒ S₈ = 3(2⁸ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 3 × 255 = **765**.

**Infinite GP:** 8 + 4 + 2 + … ⇒ r = 1/2 ⇒ S∞ = 8/(1 − 1/2) = **16** (converges only because |r| < 1).

**HP worked example:** 6, 4, 3, … ⇒ reciprocals 1/6, 1/4, 1/3 are an AP with d = 1/12 ⇒ 4th reciprocal = 5/12 ⇒ 4th HP term = **12/5**.

**AGP** (arithmetic × geometric, e.g. 1, 2r, 3r², …): find the sum using the S − rS shift method.

**Common trap:** using rⁿ instead of (rⁿ − 1) in the GP sum, or applying S∞ when |r| ≥ 1 (it does not converge).
keyPoints: GP: aₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
Infinite GP sum S∞ = a/(1 − r) is valid only when |r| < 1.
HP: take reciprocals → they form an AP → solve → invert back.
AGP = arithmetic × geometric; sum via the S − rS shift technique.

items.title: Polynomials — Remainder & Factor Theorems
items.body:
**Remainder Theorem:** when a polynomial f(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder equals **f(a)** — just substitute, no long division needed.

**Factor Theorem:** (x − a) is a factor of f(x) **iff f(a) = 0**.

**Worked example:** remainder of 2x³ − 3x² + 4x − 7 divided by (x − 2):
f(2) = 2(8) − 3(4) + 4(2) − 7 = 16 − 12 + 8 − 7 = **5**.

For a divisor (ax − b), evaluate f(b/a).

**Common trap:** substituting x = −a instead of x = +a for a divisor (x − a); also arithmetic sign slips on the constant term.
keyPoints: Remainder Theorem: remainder of f(x) ÷ (x − a) = f(a).
Factor Theorem: (x − a) is a factor iff f(a) = 0.
For divisor (ax − b), evaluate f(b/a).
Divisor (x − a) ⇒ substitute x = +a (not −a).
No long division needed — direct substitution gives the remainder.

items.title: Sets & Two-Set Venn Counting
items.body:
**Inclusion–Exclusion (two sets):** n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

- Only A = n(A) − n(A ∩ B); Only B = n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
- Neither = Universal − n(A ∪ B).
- Complement: n(A′) = n(U) − n(A).

**Worked example:** 100 students, 60 cricket, 45 tennis, 20 both.
n(C ∪ T) = 60 + 45 − 20 = 85 ⇒ Neither = 100 − 85 = **15**.

**Three sets (for reference):** n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(C∩A) + n(A∩B∩C).

**Common trap:** forgetting to add back the intersection once (double-subtracting the 'both' group), or omitting the 'neither' region from the universal total.
keyPoints: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Neither = Universal set − n(A ∪ B).
Only A = n(A) − n(A ∩ B).
Three sets add back the triple intersection n(A∩B∩C).
Complement n(A′) = n(U) − n(A).
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Sets and Type of Sets / Complement of Sets

items.title: Percentage embedded in a simplification (solve for x)
items.body:
Exam simplification items often hide one unknown percentage in an equation of the form  p₁% of A + x% of B = p₂% of C. Convert every '% of' to a product (k% of N = kN/100), collect the known terms, and solve the resulting linear equation for x.

*Example:* 25% of 480 + 30% of 500 + x% of 90 = 35% of 900.
120 + 150 + 0.9x = 315 ⇒ 0.9x = 45 ⇒ **x = 50**.

**Method:** (1) turn each percentage into a decimal-times-value, (2) move constants to the right, (3) divide by the coefficient of x.

**Trap:** 'x% of 90' is 0.9x, NOT 90x; keep the /100 on the unknown term too.
keyPoints: k% of N = kN/100; apply to the unknown term as well
Collect known products, then solve the linear equation for x
Common slip: writing x% of 90 as 90x instead of 0.9x
